lead: Both readings today ask where the power in a Christian life comes from. In Corinth the believers were boasting about their teachers, “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”; Paul answers that teachers only plant and water, and that “God gave the growth.” In the Gospel two blind men follow Jesus and cry for mercy, and he answers “According to your faith let it be done to you.” In both, the work belongs to God, and our part is to serve him and trust him. The key words are growth and faith.

set: Paul founded the Church in Corinth about AD 50–51 and stayed there for a year and a half (Acts 18:1–11). Afterwards Apollos came, a learned Jew from Alexandria, powerful in the Scriptures and in speech (Acts 18:24–28). When Paul writes from Ephesus a few years later, the community has split into parties: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”, “I belong to Cephas”, “I belong to Christ” (1:12). Some people compared the teachers like favourite athletes.
In 3:1–4 Paul has told them that this rivalry shows how immature they still are. In our verses he gives a picture from the farm to put the teachers in their place, and to put God in his.
str: v. 5: who are Apollos and Paul? Servants, each with the task the Lord gave.
v. 6: Paul planted, Apollos watered, God gave the growth.
v. 7: so the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing beside God.
v. 8: planter and waterer share one purpose, and each will receive a reward for his own labour.
v. 9: we are God’s servants working together; you are God’s field and God’s building.
kw: The word means one who serves at table or carries out a task for another. Paul and Apollos are not rival masters but servants. Our word “deacon” comes from it.
Paul uses it twice, in verses 6 and 7. In verse 6 the Greek tense (“God was giving the growth”) suggests that God keeps on giving it, long after the planting and the watering are done.
The Greek says literally “God’s fellow workers”. Paul does not make us equals of God; he says that God has chosen to carry out his work through human helpers, and that they labour together under him.
vv: What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each.
Paul asks “what”, not “who”. The question reduces the teachers to their role. Each has a task the Lord has assigned, and none of them has a task of his own choosing.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.

Paul’s own work was the first preaching and the founding of the community; the work of Apollos was to teach and strengthen it. Both were necessary, and both were small beside the living power that makes a seed grow.
So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
This is not an insult to Paul or Apollos. It releases them, and us, from the weight of thinking that the Church lives by the talent of its leaders.
The one who plants and the one who waters have a common purpose, and each will receive wages according to the labor of each.

The Greek says that planter and waterer “are one”. There is no ranking among them. The reward is real, and it is given to each “according to the labor”. The Church teaches that even this merit is itself a gift of God’s grace (CCC 2008).
you are God’s field, God’s building.
Two images follow. The field is the Church seen as a living, growing thing; the building, which Paul develops in 3:10–17, shows her as a house with one foundation, Jesus Christ.
ch: The Church has always taken these verses as a lesson on how she grows. The Catechism says that the Church is God’s “tilled field”, and that the building of God is built on Christ the cornerstone (CCC 755–756). The Second Vatican Council gathers images such as the field and the building to describe the Church (Lumen Gentium 6). Priests, parents and catechists take comfort from verse 6: they sow and water, but the growth is God’s work, and the harvest will be seen in his time. And because the planter and the waterer have “a common purpose”, rivalry among those who serve in a parish is a sign that something has been forgotten.

set: This is the second of a series of healings that Matthew gathers in chapters 8–9. It comes straight after the raising of the daughter of the synagogue leader and the healing of the woman with the flow of blood (9:18–26). Matthew likes pairs: he mentions two blind men here, and two again at Jericho (20:29–34), where Mark tells of one, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). The next story, a mute man who speaks, closes the series (9:32–34).

The cry of the blind men, “Son of David”, is the first time in Matthew that anyone other than the narrator gives Jesus this title in a healing story. It is the title of the promised king from David’s line, and the prophets said that in his time “the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isaiah 35:5).
str: v. 27: two blind men follow Jesus, crying for mercy to the Son of David.
v. 28: in the house Jesus asks, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” and they answer, “Yes, Lord.”
v. 29: he touches their eyes: “According to your faith let it be done to you.”
vv. 30b–31: he orders silence, and they spread his fame throughout the district.
kw: The Greek of the cry is eleēson hēmas, “have mercy on us”, the same word as in the “Kyrie eleison” of the liturgy. It asks for help from someone who has the power and the kindness to give it.
Jesus puts faith before healing. He asks first whether they trust that he is able, and their “Yes, Lord” shows that they call him more than a healer: they call him “Lord”.
A strong verb, used of a stern warning (see also Mark 1:43). Jesus does not want his healing to be known as the work of a wonder-worker before people understand who he is and what road he will take.
vv: two blind men followed him, crying loudly, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”
The men cannot see, but they know who he is. The prayer is short and complete: a title that confesses his identity, and a request that trusts his kindness.
“Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.”
Jesus’ question is not a test of their cleverness. It invites them to say, out loud, what they hope for. Their answer is simple, and nothing more is demanded.
“According to your faith let it be done to you.”
These words do not make faith a kind of magic power that forces God’s hand. Jesus is the one who heals; their faith opens their hands to receive what only he can give.
Then Jesus sternly ordered them, “See that no one knows of this.”

In Matthew Jesus often asks for silence about his miracles (8:4; 12:16). He does not wish to be seen only as a wonder-worker, or as an earthly king, before the cross and the resurrection have been revealed.
But they went away and spread the news about him throughout that district.
They do not obey. It is hard to blame people who have just received their sight for speaking, and Matthew records it without a word of reproach. Good news cannot be locked in.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ miracles are signs that invite faith in him; to those who come to him in faith, he grants what they ask (CCC 548). The Fathers of the Church often read the healing of the blind as a picture of the enlightenment of Baptism, when the eyes of the heart are opened to see Christ (in substance). In the Syriac liturgy the cry of the two men continues in every Holy Qurbono, when the people sing again and again “Kurielaison”, “Lord, have mercy”. The cry is not only for physical sight. We ask that he open our eyes to see his will, and the neighbour in need.

qa: If healing comes “according to your faith”, does a person who is not healed lack faith?

No. Jesus’ words are a promise to these two men, not a rule that every sick person will be cured if his or her faith is strong enough. The Church teaches that God hears every prayer, but his answer is his own: sometimes healing, sometimes strength to carry the cross, and always his closeness. Saint Paul prayed three times that a “thorn” be taken from him, and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). To say that an illness shows a lack of faith would add suffering to the sick.
study: Paul says that he planted and Apollos watered, and that God gave the growth. Who has planted or watered in my faith, and for whom do I do so?
The two blind men were asked, “Do you believe?” What would I answer if Jesus asked me today, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?”, about the greatest need in my life?
